original_value: Objective The study examines the effects of disclosing different types of likelihood information on human operators’ trust in automation, their compliance and reliance behaviors, and the human-automation team performance. Background To facilitate appropriate trust in and dependence on automation, explicitly conveying the likelihood of automation success has been proposed as one solution. Empirical studies have been conducted to investigate the potential benefits of disclosing likelihood information in the form of automation reliability, (un)certainty, and confidence. Yet, results from these studies are rather mixed. Method We conducted a human-in-the-loop experiment with 60 participants using a simulated surveillance task. Each participant performed a compensatory tracking task and a threat detection task with the help of an imperfect automated threat detector. Three types of likelihood information were presented: overall likelihood information, predictive values, and hit and correct rejection rates. Participants’ trust in automation, compliance and reliance behaviors, and task performance were measured. Results Human operators informed of the predictive values or the overall likelihood value, rather than the hit and correct rejection rates, relied on the decision aid more appropriately and obtained higher task scores. Conclusion Not all likelihood information is equal in aiding human-automation team performance. Directly presenting the hit and correct rejection rates of an automated decision aid should be avoided. Application The findings can be applied to the design of automated decision aids.

result.paraphrase: Objective This study investigates how disclosing different kinds of likelihood information affects human operators’ trust in automation, their compliance and reliance behaviors, and overall human-automation team performance. Background To promote appropriate trust in and reliance on automation, one proposed approach is to explicitly communicate the likelihood that automation will succeed. Prior empirical work has examined possible benefits of presenting likelihood information as automation reliability, (un)certainty, and confidence, but the findings have been mixed. Method We ran a human-in-the-loop experiment with 60 participants in a simulated surveillance task. Each participant completed a compensatory tracking task and a threat detection task with assistance from an imperfect automated threat detector. Three likelihood-information formats were shown: overall likelihood information, predictive values, and hit and correct rejection rates. We measured participants’ trust in automation, compliance and reliance behaviors, and task performance. Results Participants given the predictive values or the overall likelihood value, rather than the hit and correct rejection rates, used the decision aid more appropriately and achieved higher task scores. Conclusion Not all likelihood information contributes equally to human-automation team performance. Direct presentation of an automated decision aid’s hit and correct rejection rates should be avoided. Application These findings can inform the design of automated decision aids.
